newsitem.title: UK: Political worries seen braking UK stocks next week.
newsitem.headline: Political worries seen braking UK stocks next week.

text.p: After a week when the UK's FTSE 100 punched through the 4,000 point barrier to record highs, equity strategists said consolidation was on the cards for next week.

The market spiked higher on Friday after a surprise drop in U.S. payrolls sent global debt markets soaring. Later it seemed to seek shelter close to 4,000 -- which strategists saw as its likely haven next week from economic and political concerns.
"We'll probably see the market oscillate around 4,000 and then a period of consolidation," said Roger Monson, chief equity strategist at Daiwa Europe.
"There is then the problem of the looming election and I believe investors have not yet fully discounted what a Labour government could mean," Monson added.
The market had a taste of those political worries earlier this week as investors ran scared on a Labour Party threat of a windfall tax on privatised utilities.
That braked the market initially, but it quickly gathered steam over the week on the back of a rally in gilts and an influx of investment fund cash.
The FTSE cruised through 4,000 points on Wednesday and set a record 4,024.3 points on Thursday.
The upswing was partly helped by bullishness on P&O's short-sea ferry merger with its rival Swedish line Stena and takeover speculation around Imperial Tobacco.
Although trading volumes were healthy, at least early in the week, experts said the market seemed to have come off the boil amid a wave of profit-taking.
"The difficulty is that the market has already rallied by roughly 10 percent since July and there are quite a few profits to be taken," said Morgan Stanley's Kevin Gardner.
But experts said the market remained on a sound footing, especially based on the lastest economic signals from the U.S..
The latest U.S. payroll data, and favourable comments on inflation this week from U.S. Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, have allayed interest rate fears and underpinned debt markets.
Traders said several UK investment houses were contemplating revising upwards their year-end forecasts for the FTSE, helped by bullish outlooks for general manufacturing.
But the market next week was unlikely to repeat this week's run which saw the FTSE gain over 60 points.
Richard Jeffrey, strategist at Charterhouse Tilney, also felt political worries would nag at investors, while Monday's output figures and Thursday retail prices could spur caution.

"There is concern the economy is running a little fast," Jeffrey said. "Inflation hasn't fallen perhaps as quickly as wanted. If output and manufacturing figures show too sharp an improvement and retail prices come in high, that could worry people."

Philip Isherwood, strategist at Kleinwort Benson, said the market was likely to hold 4,000 for the time being and could wobble slightly on the UK retail price figures, despite being on course for 4,200 by year-end.
He added that he believed most of the political risk from a potential Labour government was priced into the market.

Isherwood argued that that risk had not intensified despite "many questions remaining unanswered". But he did not doubt that politics would remain at the forefront with the Conservative Party conference running next week.
Traders said the market lacked incentives to push higher, with little on the corporate calendar to foster interest.

Only a handful of companies report next week, including Moss Bros, Tay Homes, newly merged LucasVarity and football club Manchester United. Deutsche Morgan Grenfell releases half-year results on Thursday.
